QtFL Ternary Diagram for Provenance Analysis

Source: R/ternary_dickinson_qtfl.R
ternary_dickinson_qtfl.Rd

ternary_dickinson_qtfl() draws either a static or interactive ternary diagram, in english or spanish. It is a base diagram where data can be plotted.

Usage

ternary_dickinson_qtfl(
  output = c("ggplot", "plotly"),
  language = c("en", "es"),
  opacity = 0.5
)

Arguments

output

The output format: "ggplot" or "plotly" (default is "ggplot")

language

The language to be displayed: "en" for english or "es" for spanish (deafult is "en")

opacity

Transparency level (default is 0.5)

Value

QtFL ternary diagram for provenance analysis in the desired format (object)

Details

For plotting data on the ggplot object it would be easier if the names of the dataframe are "f", "qt", and "l", that way it gets mapped automatically, if not make sure to use "aes(x=f,y=qt,z=l)". For plotting on the plotly object the mapping of the new data should be as shown in the example: a = ~qt, b = ~f, c = ~l, where a refers to the top ("qt"), b refers to the bottom left ("f"), and c refers to the bottom right ("l"). The examples show basic usage and how to add data, which can be more customizable. For a more complete description on how to use this function and similar ones, see vignette("classification_diagrams_vig")

The QtFL diagram is used in sedimentary petrology to classify sandstones based on their detrital composition, specifically the relative proportions of quartz (Qt), feldspar (F), and lithic fragments (L). The diagram helps to infer the tectonic setting and provenance of the sedimentary rocks, as different source areas and geological processes produce characteristic detrital assemblages.

The QtFL diagram was proposed by Dickinson (1985) as a modification of the traditional QFL diagram, which only considers quartz, feldspar, and lithic fragments. The QtFL diagram includes a fourth component, "Qt", which represents the total quartz content (including both monocrystalline and polycrystalline quartz). This allows for a more accurate classification of sandstones, especially those with high quartz content, and provides better insights into the sedimentary processes and source areas.

See also

Examples

library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

d = data.frame(qt=c(23,40,60),
               f=c(27,50,30),
               l=c(50,10,10),
               loc=c("A", "B", "C"))

# adding data to ggplot object
ternary_dickinson_qtfl() + geom_point(aes(col = loc), data = d)
#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • T : "Qt"
#> • L : "F"
#> • R : "L"


# adding data to plotly object
ternary_dickinson_qtfl('plotly') %>%
  add_trace(a = ~qt, b = ~f, c = ~l,
            data = d,
            name = 'My data',
            type = "scatterternary",
            mode = "markers",
            marker = list(size=8,color='coral',symbol=3,opacity=.9),
            hovertemplate = paste0('Qt: %{a}<br>',
                                   'F: %{b}<br>',
                                   'L: %{c}'))



# adding data to plotly object with custom colors
my_pal    <- c("A" = "red",      "B" = "blue",   "C" = "green")
my_shapes <- c("A" = "circle",   "B" = "square",  "C" = "diamond")

ternary_dickinson_qtfl('plotly') %>%
  add_trace(a = ~qt, b = ~f, c = ~l,
            data = d,
            type = "scatterternary",
            mode = "markers",
            split = ~loc,
            marker = list(size=8,
                          color  = ~my_pal[loc],
                          symbol = ~my_shapes[loc],
                          opacity=.9),
            hovertemplate = paste0('Qt: %{a}<br>',
                                   'F: %{b}<br>',
                                   'L: %{c}'))
